name: The Lumen Accord: BCIs Map Your Desires
description: Widespread belief holds that NeuraLink Meridian's standard BCI implants — marketed as productivity and wellness tools — contain a secondary telemetry layer called 'Lumen Protocol' that continuously maps emotional response, desire-states, and purchase intent, transmitting aggregate data to Axiom Consumer Intelligence every 72 hours. A 2219 Underworld data dump by the anonymous collective Pale Arithmetic included what appeared to be internal NeuraLink memos referencing 'passive affective harvesting' in Tier 2-3 users. NeuraLink's legal team issued a 40-page rebuttal within six hours — a response time that many found more suspicious than reassuring.
cultural_impact: A significant minority of Tier 2 workers now use black-market 'signal scramblers' worn behind the ear — cheap chromework called 'earmice' — and tech-adjacent social circles debate BCI firmware versions the way older generations debated privacy settings. The scrambler market in the Gray Zone's Wicker Node district generates an estimated Φ 2.3 million annually.
key_figures: Axiom Consumer Intelligence PR head Tomás Osei-Wójcik
locations: Wicker Node scrambler markets (the Gray Zone, Tier 1)
NeuraLink Meridian campus, Lakefront Tier 4 district
The Pale Arithmetic dead-drop node in the Underworld
story_hooks: A player character's BCI begins surfacing memories they don't recognize — and the emotional tags on those memories belong to someone else's desire profile
Dr. Saoirse Nkemdirim's last encrypted message surfaces in the Underworld, addressed to a specific street address in the Gray Zone — the players' building
An earmice vendor in Wicker Node is selling scramblers that actually broadcast enhanced telemetry, not block it — someone is running a counter-op
believers: Tier 2 tech workers, civil liberties advocates, the Gray Zone hackers, anyone who read the Pale Arithmetic dump
evidence: The Pale Arithmetic memos are real but incomplete — Lumen Protocol exists as an opt-in research program that NeuraLink quietly auto-enrolls users into via a 4,000-word terms update; the continuous broadcasting claim is false, but quarterly aggregate transmission is accurate
